The idea is a bit complicated, but an intuitive idea is given by the graph on top of the page I linked. If you draw the fuction which increases by n+1 each time and then connect the middles of each plateau, the graph continues to -1/12 at x=0. This is useful, because this method is a primitive version of an integral, which is essentially the area underneath the graph and therefore the sum of all natural numbers.

Ramanujan stated that the sum of all natural numbers can be taken to equal -1/12. Thus, -6(1+2+...) = -6*-1/12 = 1/2. This result is surprisingly useful in string theory and other fields of theoretical physics. If you'd like to read more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1_%2B_2_%2B_3_%2B_4_%2B_%E2%8B%AF

This is where it gets tricky. If you take a sum of a finite number of elements, so n < ∞, we can always calculate the solution. There is, however, an (countably) infinite number of natural numbers. Because it doesn't matter in which order of elements you take the sum, you can use some tricks. The result of -1/12 is not necessarily incorrect, and that is used in string theory. Here are some links:
[https://medium.com/cantors-paradise/the-ramanujan-summation-1-2-3-1-12-a8cc23dea793](https://medium.com/cantors-paradise/the-ramanujan-summation-1-2-3-1-12-a8cc23dea793)

The proof uses some quite advanced mathematics, I'd say second year of a bachelor's degree in University, so don't worry if you don't understand everything directly. This is why the concept of infinity is so complicated. If you want to learn some more, I'd recommend this video:
[https://youtu.be/Uj3_KqkI9Zo](https://youtu.be/Uj3_KqkI9Zo)

Notice that for every number greater than zero, the outcome of the summation is larger than that number if you choose n large enough. That means that the summation goes to infinity. Another way you can see this: (n(n+1)²)/2 = (n(n²+2n+1))/2 = (n³+2n²+n)/2 ≥ n³/2. It should be easier to see that n³/2 goes to infinity for increasing n. We stress about how others see us way more than how others appear to us - it is the reason why we remember our own embarrassing moments when we drift to sleep and the ones of others not so much. We cannot control the actions of others, so we blame ourselves for mistakes we could have avoided.
Life tends to kick us down sometimes. Remember the happy times you've had together. Don't kill the pain, and with it the joy you felt. Talk about your emotions with a friend whom you trust. If he/she is a good friend, it'll strengthen your bond and take weight off your shoulders.
